section.title: The Burning Bush
section.sectionRationale: One long call narrative unified by the theophany at the bush and Moses' five successive objections, each answered by God, until Aaron is appointed as spokesman in 4:14-17. This is the seam between Moses' private exile and his public mission.
section.thesis: The God who sees His people's affliction reveals His covenant name, I AM, and sends a reluctant, self-doubting shepherd to confront the most powerful throne on earth, proving that the mission rests on who God is, not on who Moses is.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the bush that burns but is not consumed; God's commission and self-revelation of His name; Moses' objections and God's signs; the naming of Aaron as spokesman.

units.label: The bush that is not consumed

verses.text: Meanwhile, Moses was shepherding the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a blazing fire from within a bush. Moses saw the bush ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed.
So Moses thought, “I must go over and see this marvelous sight. Why is the bush not burning up?”
When the LORD saw that he had gone over to look, God called out to him from within the bush, “Moses, Moses!” “Here I am,” he answered.
“Do not come any closer,” God said. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is {{qodesh|holy ground}}.”
Then He said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” At this, Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.

units.label: I have seen, I have heard, I will send you

verses.text: The LORD said, “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors, and I am aware of their sufferings.

I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey, the home of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
And now the cry of the Israelites has reached Me, and I have seen how severely the Egyptians are oppressing them.
Therefore, go! I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring My people the Israelites out of Egypt.”
But Moses asked God, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?”
“I will surely be with you,” God said, “and this will be the sign to you that I have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, all of you will worship God on this mountain.”
Then Moses asked God, “Suppose I go to the Israelites and say to them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is His name?’ What should I tell them?”
God said to Moses, “{{ehyeh|I AM WHO I AM}}. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

God also told Moses, “Say to the Israelites, ‘The {{yhwh|LORD}}, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered in every generation.

Go, assemble the elders of Israel and say to them, ‘The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, has appeared to me and said: I have surely attended to you and have seen what has been done to you in Egypt.
And I have promised to bring you up out of your affliction in Egypt, into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey.’

The elders of Israel will listen to what you say, and you must go with them to the king of Egypt and tell him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Now please let us take a three-day journey into the wilderness, so that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.’
But I know that the king of Egypt will not allow you to go unless a mighty hand compels him.
So I will stretch out My hand and strike the Egyptians with all the wonders I will perform among them. And after that, he will release you.
And I will grant this people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that when you leave, you will not go away empty-handed.
Every woman shall ask her neighbor and any woman staying in her house for silver and gold jewelry and clothing, and you will put them on your sons and daughters. So you will plunder the Egyptians.”

units.label: Signs for the doubting shepherd
units.note: staff, hand, and water; Aaron as spokesman

verses.text: Then Moses answered, “What if they do not believe me or listen to my voice? For they may say, ‘The LORD has not appeared to you.’”
And the LORD asked him, “What is that in your hand?” “A staff,” he replied.
“Throw it on the ground,” said the LORD. So Moses threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and he ran from it.
“Stretch out your hand and grab it by the tail,” the LORD said to Moses, who reached out his hand and caught the snake, and it turned back into a staff in his hand.
“This is so that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.”
Furthermore, the LORD said to Moses, “Put your hand inside your cloak.” So he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, his hand was leprous, white as snow.
“Put your hand back inside your cloak,” said the LORD. So Moses put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, it was restored, like the rest of his skin.
And the LORD said, “If they refuse to believe you or heed the witness of the first sign, they may believe that of the second.

But if they do not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground. Then the water you take from the Nile will become blood on the ground.”
“Please, Lord,” Moses replied, “I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since You have spoken to Your servant, for I am slow of speech and tongue.”
And the LORD said to him, “Who gave man his mouth? Or who makes the mute or the deaf, the sighted or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD?
Now go! I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.”
But Moses replied, “Please, Lord, send someone else.”

Then the anger of the LORD burned against Moses, and He said, “Is not Aaron the Levite your brother? I know that he can speak well, and he is now on his way to meet you. When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.
You are to speak to him and put the words in his mouth. I will help both of you to speak, and I will teach you what to do.
He will speak to the people for you. He will be your spokesman, and it will be as if you were God to him.”
But take this staff in your hand so you can perform signs with it.”

qodesh.gloss: Holy, set apart. The ground itself is not magical, but it is set apart by God's presence, the first time the word appears in Scripture attached to a physical place, anticipating tabernacle and temple.

ehyeh.gloss: I AM WHO I AM, or I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE. From the verb hayah, to be. God declares Himself self-existent, dependent on nothing, utterly reliable, and present with His people in whatever the moment requires.

yhwh.gloss: The LORD, God's personal covenant name, built from the same root as ehyeh, I AM. Traditionally read aloud as Adonai out of reverence, it is God's name forever, the name by which He is to be remembered in every generation.

basic.context: After forty years as a shepherd in Midian, Moses meets God at a bush that burns without burning up. God tells him He has seen Israel's suffering and is sending Moses to confront Pharaoh and lead the people out of Egypt. Moses objects five times, and God patiently answers each objection, finally allowing Aaron to speak for him.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical encounter, not a symbol or myth. The heart of the passage is God's self-revelation of His name and character, and it teaches that God's call does not depend on the qualifications of the one He calls, but on who He is.
basic.originalLanguages: God announces His name as Ehyeh asher ehyeh, I AM WHO I AM, built on the Hebrew verb to be. From this comes YHWH, the LORD, His personal covenant name forever. He is self-existent and utterly reliable, the God who simply is, and who will be present with His people however the moment requires.
basic.typology: The bush that burns yet is not consumed pictures God's holy presence dwelling with His people without destroying them, a pattern fulfilled when the Word became flesh and dwelt among sinners without being consumed by their sin, and when the Spirit indwells believers as a holy, undestroying fire.
basic.christ: Jesus takes the divine name for Himself, saying before Abraham was, I AM, John 8:58, provoking His hearers precisely because they understood the claim. He is the true and greater deliverer, sent not merely to bring people out of Egypt but out of slavery to sin, and He, unlike Moses, never once refuses the mission the Father gives Him.
basic.god: God is self-existent, compassionate, and covenant-keeping. He sees affliction, hears crying, and comes down to rescue, and He reveals His eternal name precisely at the moment He commits to act in history for His people.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 7:30-34 retells this scene in Stephen's speech. John 8:58 has Jesus claiming the I AM. Matthew 22:32 has Jesus citing verse 6 to prove the resurrection, since God is the God of the living.
basic.oneStory: This is the ignition point of the exodus: the God who kept His covenant reveals His eternal name and commissions a reluctant deliverer. It anticipates the whole redemptive pattern fulfilled in Christ, the great I AM who comes down to rescue His people from a bondage deeper than Egypt's.

context.literary:
Exodus 3:1-4:17 is the longest conversation between God and a human being in the Pentateuch up to this point, and it follows a shape the Bible will use again. Scholars often call it a call narrative: God confronts, God commissions, the one called objects, God reassures with a promise of His presence, and God gives a sign. The same pattern appears with Gideon, who protests 'how can I save Israel?' and hears 'Surely I will be with you,' Judges 6:15-16, and with Jeremiah, who pleads that he does not know how to speak, Jeremiah 1:6-9.

Here the objection stage is stretched out on purpose. Moses raises five objections: who am I, 3:11; what is Your name, 3:13; what if they do not believe me, 4:1; I am not eloquent, 4:10; and finally, please send someone else, 4:13. The first four are questions that God answers. The fifth is not a question at all, and it is the only one that provokes God's anger, 4:14. The sequence moves from humility, through doubt, to plain refusal.

The scene is also framed by seeing. It begins with a sight Moses turns aside to look at, 3:3, and the LORD 'saw that he had gone over to look,' 3:4. Moses hides his face because he is afraid to look at God, 3:6, and God's first words of mission are 'I have indeed seen,' 3:7. The man who looked this way and that before killing the Egyptian, Exodus 2:12, now learns to look at the God who sees.

The divine speech in 3:7-10 answers Exodus 2:23-25 point for point: seen, heard, aware, the cry reaching Him. The narrator's report becomes God's own voice. Then the verb turns: 'I have come down,' 3:8, but 'I am sending you,' 3:10. God's descent will happen through a human messenger. The unit closes where it began, with the staff in Moses' hand, 4:17, the ordinary shepherd's tool that will become 'the staff of God.'
context.historical:
Moses is now around eighty, Exodus 7:7, working another man's flock. Leading it 'to the far side of the wilderness,' 3:1, suggests a long seasonal migration in search of pasture. Horeb is called 'the mountain of God' before anything has happened there, because the narrator writes knowing what it will become. The BSB footnote identifies it with Mount Sinai or the range around it. Its location is uncertain: church tradition placed it in the southern Sinai peninsula, while others look east of the Gulf of Aqaba, nearer Midian, noting Paul's phrase 'Mount Sinai in Arabia,' Galatians 4:25. The text does not settle it.

Removing sandals was a gesture of reverence and of lowliness; Joshua is told the same at Jericho, Joshua 5:15. Sandals carry the dust of ordinary ground, and holy ground is not ordinary.

The list of nations in 3:8 and 3:17, Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, names the peoples of the land promised to Abraham in Genesis 15:18-21. 'Milk and honey' describes a land rich in pasture and wild bees or fruit syrup, a shepherd's picture of abundance, quite different from the river-watered fields of Egypt.

The signs speak Egypt's own language. The cobra was a well known emblem of Pharaoh's royal power, worn on the crown, and here a snake is turned back into a staff by the hand of God's messenger. The Nile was Egypt's life source, and water from it turning to blood anticipates the first plague, Exodus 7:17-21. The request for a three-day journey to sacrifice, 3:18, asked for something Pharaoh could grant without losing his workforce for good. God already knows he will not, 3:19.

In the ancient world a name was more than a label. It was thought to disclose character and to give the one who knew it a way to call on its bearer. Moses' question in 3:13 is not only 'what do we call You?' but 'who are You, and what will You do?'
context.canonical:
The bush is remembered at the end of the Torah. Moses blesses Joseph with 'the favor of Him who dwelt in the burning bush,' Deuteronomy 33:16. The fire returns at Sinai itself, where the LORD descended 'in fire' and the mountain smoked like a furnace, Exodus 19:18, and the glory on the mountain looked 'like a consuming fire,' Exodus 24:17. Elijah fled to 'Horeb, the mountain of God,' 1 Kings 19:8, returning to the place where the covenant began.

The name revealed here becomes the centre of Israel's faith. God tells Moses in Exodus 6:2-3 that He appeared to the patriarchs as God Almighty but did not make Himself known to them by His name the LORD, meaning they had not yet experienced what the name would mean in redemption. He proclaims the name's content in Exodus 34:5-7: compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. Hosea calls it 'His name of renown,' Hosea 12:5, and in Isaiah the LORD says, 'I am He... I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me,' Isaiah 43:10-11.

The New Testament quotes the passage often. Stephen retells it, Acts 7:30-34. Jesus uses 3:6 to answer the Sadducees: God said 'I am the God of Abraham,' and He 'is not the God of the dead, but of the living,' Mark 12:26-27, with parallels in Matthew 22:32 and Luke 20:37. John's Gospel echoes the divine 'I am' in Jesus' own words, John 8:58 and 18:5-6. Revelation names God as the one 'who is and was and is to come,' Revelation 1:4 and 1:8, a phrase widely heard as an expansion of Exodus 3:14. Hebrews closes its contrast between Sinai and Zion by saying 'our God is a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:29, the fire of the bush and the mountain still burning.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses records his own reluctance without softening it. He wants Israel to know that the man who led them out did not volunteer. He argued, stalled and finally asked God to send someone else. If the exodus had depended on Moses' courage or eloquence, it would never have happened. The author means Israel to see that their redemption was God's initiative from beginning to end.

He also wants Israel to know God's name and what it means. The generation that left Egypt had lived for centuries among gods who were many, local and bound to images. The name given at the bush tells them that their God is not one of these. He is the God of their fathers, present in every generation, 3:15, the one who has seen and come down. When they later sang, 'The LORD is His name,' they were singing what was revealed here.

Finally, the author wants Israel to trust God's promise of presence more than their own adequacy. Four times God answers an objection not by improving Moses but by pointing to Himself: I will be with you, I AM, I made the mouth, I will teach you. The lesson for every hearer is that the question 'Who am I?' is answered by 'I will be with you.'
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes a unique event. No one else is told to remove their sandals before this bush, hears the name revealed for the first time, or receives these particular signs. Believers should not expect burning bushes, and the signs given to Moses were for the authentication of his mission to Israel and Pharaoh, 4:5 and 4:8.

Yet much here carries forward. The reverence of 3:5-6 remains the right posture before a holy God, and Hebrews 12:28-29 calls believers to worship 'with reverence and awe.' The pattern of calling still teaches: God's servants are not chosen because they are sufficient, and the answer to inadequacy is His presence, as Jesus promised His disciples that the Spirit would give them words, Matthew 10:19-20. Moses' fifth objection is a warning. Honest questions are welcomed, but a settled refusal dressed as humility angers the LORD, 4:14. And the plundering of Egypt, 3:21-22, is not a license for taking others' goods; it is God's specific provision, the wages owed to a people enslaved for generations, and it was given freely by the Egyptians, Exodus 12:35-36.

debates.question: What exactly does the divine name I AM WHO I AM mean?

views.label: Absolute self-existence
views.case: God is declaring His eternal, uncaused being, dependent on nothing, the ground of all other existence. The Septuagint rendered the phrase 'I am the one who is,' and much of the church, from the fathers to the Reformers, heard in it God's aseity and unchangeableness.

views.label: I will be what I will be, active presence
views.case: The Hebrew verb form is imperfect and can carry a future sense, as the BSB footnote notes: 'I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.' The same form, ehyeh, appears in 3:12, 'I will surely be with you.' On this reading God is promising to be present and active for His people however the moment requires, not giving a metaphysical definition.

views.label: A sovereign reserve
views.case: Some hear in the circular phrase a refusal to be pinned down: God will be who He chooses to be, and Israel cannot manage or manipulate Him by knowing His name, as the nations tried to manage their gods. He reveals Himself, but on His terms.

debates.bearing: The readings are not rivals. The God who simply is, dependent on nothing, is for that very reason free to be faithfully present with His people, and free from their control. The name grounds Israel's confidence: He is utterly reliable and personally engaged in their deliverance.

debates.question: Who is the angel of the LORD in the bush?

views.label: A created angel speaking for God
views.case: Messengers in the ancient world spoke in the first person for the one who sent them. On this view a created angel appears in the fire, 3:2, and delivers God's words, which is why Stephen can say God sent Moses 'through the angel who appeared to him in the bush,' Acts 7:35.

views.label: The LORD Himself appearing
views.case: The text moves without a break from 'the angel of the LORD appeared,' 3:2, to 'God called out to him from within the bush,' 3:4, and the speaker says, 'I am the God of your father,' 3:6. Moses hides his face from God. The angel is not distinct from the LORD in what he claims or receives.

views.label: The Son before His incarnation
views.case: Many early Christian writers identified the angel of the LORD with the eternal Son, who is both sent by the Father and Himself God. The BSB footnote allows 'Angel' with a capital. They noted that John 1:18 says the Son has made the unseen God known.

debates.bearing: The passage itself identifies the angel with God, so the first view struggles to explain 3:6. The second and third views agree that God Himself spoke from the bush. The New Testament does not explicitly name the angel as the Son, so that identification is a reasonable inference rather than a stated doctrine, but it fits the pattern of a God who is both sender and sent.

study.originalLanguages:
The 'bush' of 3:2-4 is seneh, a word that sounds very like Sinai. It reappears in Moses' blessing, 'Him who dwelt in the burning bush,' Deuteronomy 33:16, where the verb is shakan, to dwell, the root of the word for the tabernacle. The bush where God dwelt in fire anticipates the mountain of fire and the tent of meeting.

God calls 'Moses, Moses!' and Moses answers 'Here I am,' hinneni, 3:4. The doubled name and the reply belong to the great moments of calling: 'Abraham, Abraham!' Genesis 22:11, 'Jacob, Jacob!' Genesis 46:2, 'Samuel! Samuel!' 1 Samuel 3:10. Hinneni is not a statement of location but of availability. Moses' later 'Please, Lord, send someone else,' 4:13, is the reverse of this first word.

God's speech in 3:7 opens with an intensive, the infinitive beside the finite verb, ra'oh ra'iti, 'seeing I have seen,' rendered 'I have indeed seen.' It is followed by 'I am aware,' yada'ti, 'I know.' Those are the last two verbs of Exodus 2:25. In 3:16 God uses another doubled form, paqod paqadti, 'I have surely attended to you.' Joseph had died saying, 'God will surely attend to you,' Genesis 50:25, the same verb and the same construction. The bush is the answer to Joseph's deathbed promise.

Most important for the name itself is the verb in 3:12. Moses asks, 'Who am I?' mi anokhi. God answers, 'I will surely be with you,' ehyeh immak. Two verses later the name is ehyeh asher ehyeh, and the short form 'I AM has sent me' is simply ehyeh, 3:14. God's name is given first as a promise of presence before it is given as a title. The same pattern returns in 4:12, 'I will help you as you speak,' literally 'I will be with your mouth,' and 4:15, 'I will help both of you to speak,' literally 'I will be with your mouth and with his mouth.' The covenant name YHWH in 3:15 is the third person form of the same verb, 'He is' or 'He will be,' and God says it is His name forever and His zekher, His memorial, the way He is to be remembered in every generation. The Septuagint rendered 3:14 ego eimi ho on, 'I am the one who is,' the wording that shaped much early Christian reflection.

Moses calls himself 'slow of speech and tongue,' 4:10, literally 'heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue,' using kaved, heavy. The same word will describe Pharaoh's heart as 'unyielding' in Exodus 7:14. The heavy-mouthed prophet will face the heavy-hearted king, and the victory will belong to neither.

Finally, 3:22 says Israel 'will plunder' the Egyptians, from natsal. In 3:8 God used the same verb for 'rescue.' In the one stem it means to snatch someone from danger; in another, to strip or despoil. God will snatch His people out, and in doing so Egypt will be stripped, Exodus 12:36.

typology.type: The bush that burns and is not consumed, Exodus 3:2
typology.fulfillment: The bush shows the holy God dwelling in something lowly without destroying it. The pattern grows through the tabernacle, where the fire of God's glory filled a tent of skins, and comes to its height when 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. In Jesus the fullness of God dwelt in a human body, not consuming it but glorifying it. The New Testament does not explicitly name the bush as a type, so this rests on the wider biblical theme of God's dwelling. The type falls short, since the bush was only a place of meeting, while Christ is God and man in one person.

typology.type: The holy ground where God meets a sinner, Exodus 3:5
typology.fulfillment: Moses must keep his distance, remove his sandals and hide his face, for 'no one can see Me and live,' Exodus 33:20. The distance is real grace, protecting him. In Christ the distance is overcome without the holiness being lessened. The Son 'has made Him known,' John 1:18, and believers draw near through His blood, Hebrews 10:19-22. Hebrews 12:18-24 contrasts the fearful mountain of fire with Mount Zion, where believers come to 'Jesus the mediator of a new covenant.' Yet the same letter adds that God remains 'a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:29. Nearness in Christ is not casualness.

God says, 'I am sending you,' and the rest of Exodus is the mission of a sent man. Jesus speaks of Himself constantly as the one the Father sent, John 5:36-38, and Hebrews calls Him 'the apostle and high priest whom we confess,' Hebrews 3:1, then compares Him with Moses: Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, Christ as the Son over it, Hebrews 3:5-6. The escalation is plain in this passage. Moses tried five times to refuse the mission, while the Son came saying, 'I have come to do Your will,' Hebrews 10:9, and never once asked the Father to send another.

typology.type: The staff in the shepherd's hand, Exodus 4:2-4, 17
typology.fulfillment: God takes the most ordinary tool Moses owns and makes it the instrument of wonders, the staff that will strike the Nile and stretch over the sea, Exodus 14:16. The pattern is that God works His rescue through what is weak and common. Paul describes the cross in those terms: 'God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise,' 1 Corinthians 1:27, and Christ crucified is 'the power of God,' 1 Corinthians 1:24. The staff was a sign pointing to God's power; the cross is that power itself, where the Shepherd was struck so that the flock might be saved.

study.christ:
The line from this passage to Christ runs first through the name. In John 8:58 Jesus says, 'Truly, truly, I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am.' His hearers pick up stones, John 8:59, because they understand that He has spoken in the voice of the bush. When soldiers come to arrest Him and He answers 'I am He,' they 'drew back and fell to the ground,' John 18:5-6. The name that made Moses hide his face is spoken by a man in a garden, and armed men cannot stand before it. Paul says God gave Jesus 'the name above all names,' so that every tongue confesses 'Jesus Christ is Lord,' Philippians 2:9-11, and he applies the LORD's promise 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' to faith in Jesus, Romans 10:13.

The passage also leads to Christ through the God who 'comes down.' In 3:8 God says, 'I have come down to rescue them.' He descended in fire and in word, but He sent Moses to do the work. In the incarnation the pattern completes itself: the One who comes down and the one who is sent are the same person. 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. The one who saw Israel's affliction in Egypt came into affliction Himself.

Jesus Himself uses this passage to teach the resurrection. When the Sadducees deny it, He reads 3:6 to them: God said 'I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,' and 'He is not the God of the dead, but of the living,' Mark 12:26-27. The covenant name implies that God's relationship with His people cannot be ended by death. Jesus draws out what the bush already held.

There is a quieter link in 4:11: 'Who gave man his mouth? Or who makes the mute or the deaf, the sighted or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD?' When Jesus opened deaf ears and loosened a tongue in the Decapolis, the crowd said, 'He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!' Mark 7:37. He did what the LORD claimed at the bush as His own prerogative. And He promised His disciples the help God promised Moses: 'I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist,' Luke 21:15.

Finally, the contrast. Moses was reluctant, and God's anger burned against him. Christ is the sent one who never refused. Hebrews 3:5-6 sets them side by side: Moses faithful as a servant, Christ faithful as the Son. The bush itself should not be pressed into a detailed allegory; the New Testament never says the fire is the Spirit or the bush is the incarnation. Its lasting link is God Himself, dwelling in fire, speaking His name, and coming down, which is what Christ fulfils.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is His holiness. The ground is holy not because of anything in the soil but because God is there, 3:5. Holiness here is not first a moral quality but a presence that sets things apart. Moses is drawn by curiosity, 3:3, and stopped by command, 3:5. God can be approached, but not on the human terms of curiosity alone.

Second, God is self-existent and self-defining. Moses asks for a name, and God answers with a sentence that only God could say of Himself, 'I AM WHO I AM.' He is not defined by anything outside Himself, not by Egypt's gods, not by Israel's expectations, not by Moses' ability. The bush that burns without fuel is an apt setting for such a name: God depends on nothing to be what He is. Theologians call this aseity, and the church has long rooted it in this verse.

Third, the self-existent God is also the God of relationship. He does not introduce Himself as an abstract being but as 'the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,' 3:6, and He says, 'This is My name forever,' 3:15. The same God who is dependent on nothing binds Himself freely to people. His transcendence does not keep Him away; it is what makes His nearness trustworthy.

Fourth, God is compassionate and active. 'I have indeed seen... I have heard... I am aware... I have come down,' 3:7-8. He is moved by affliction and takes action against it. Genesis used 'came down' of God's judgment at Babel, Genesis 11:5, and on Sodom, Genesis 18:21. Here the descent is for rescue, though it will mean judgment on Egypt too.

Fifth, God is sovereign over both human capacity and human resistance. He claims the making of mouths, eyes and ears, 4:11, and He knows beforehand that Pharaoh will not let Israel go unless a mighty hand compels him, 3:19. Neither Moses' weakness nor Pharaoh's strength is outside His rule.

The passage also holds a tension. God is patient, answering objection after objection, and He is also angry, 4:14. His anger does not cancel the call; it adds Aaron, and it keeps Moses. His patience does not mean indulgence, and His anger does not mean rejection.

For worship, the passage teaches both reverence and confidence. Believers take off their sandals, as it were, before a holy God, and they call on Him by His name as the God who has seen, come down and promised, 'I will be with you.'

crossReferences.note: Joseph died saying, 'God will surely attend to you,' and asked for his bones to be carried up. In Exodus 3:16 God tells Moses, 'I have surely attended to you,' using the same doubled construction. The bush is the fulfilment of Joseph's dying hope, and Exodus 13:19 later records the bones being carried out.

God's covenant with Abram names the land and lists the peoples who hold it, Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites and Jebusites among them. The list in Exodus 3:8 and 3:17 repeats that promise, telling Moses that the goal of the exodus is not only escape from Egypt but the land sworn to Abraham.

Gideon objects that his clan is the weakest and he the least, and the LORD answers, 'Surely I will be with you.' The call of Gideon follows the pattern of Moses' call: objection answered not by better credentials but by the promise of God's presence, the same promise as Exodus 3:12.

Jeremiah protests, 'I surely do not know how to speak,' much as Moses pleaded he was not eloquent, Exodus 4:10. The LORD touches his mouth and says, 'I have put My words in your mouth,' the same answer given to Moses in 4:12 and 4:15, and later promised of the prophet like Moses, Deuteronomy 18:18.

The LORD proclaims His own name to Moses on the same mountain: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, yet not leaving the guilty unpunished. Exodus 3 gives the name; Exodus 34 unfolds what it means. The two passages together are the heart of Israel's knowledge of God.

At the end of his life Moses blesses Joseph with 'the favor of Him who dwelt in the burning bush.' Forty years later the bush is still, for Moses, the defining picture of God. The verb dwelt links the bush to the tabernacle, where God would dwell among His people.

Jesus answers the Sadducees from 'the burning bush in the Book of Moses.' Because God called Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob long after their deaths, He is the God of the living. Jesus reads Exodus 3:6 as a pledge of resurrection hidden in the covenant name.

'Before Abraham was born, I am.' Jesus does not say 'I was' but uses the absolute 'I am,' echoing the name of Exodus 3:14. His hearers take up stones to kill Him, John 8:59, showing that they understood Him to be claiming the name spoken from the bush.

When the arresting party names Jesus of Nazareth, He answers, 'I am He,' and they draw back and fall to the ground. The words carry the weight of the divine name. As Moses hid his face at the bush, armed men cannot stand before the one who speaks it.

The crowd says of Jesus, 'He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!' In Exodus 4:11 the LORD claims as His own the making of the mute, the deaf, the sighted and the blind. Jesus does in the flesh what the LORD claimed at the bush as His prerogative.

Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house; Christ is faithful as the Son over it. Hebrews honours Moses and then places him below Christ. The reluctant servant of Exodus 3 and 4 points to the Son who came willingly to do the Father's will.

The letter closes its comparison of Sinai and Zion by calling believers to worship with reverence and awe, 'for our God is a consuming fire.' The fire that did not consume the bush is still the fire of God's holiness, and it shapes how believers approach Him even under grace.

The Lord God calls Himself 'the Alpha and the Omega... who is and was and is to come.' The phrase is widely heard as an expansion of the name I AM, spanning past, present and future, the God who was with the fathers and will be with His people forever.

study.oneStory:
At the start of the Bible, God walked with humanity in a garden and was known face to face. After the fall, humanity hid from His presence, and the way back was guarded by cherubim with a flaming sword, Genesis 3:24. Fire and holiness stood between sinners and God. Now, at the bush, God appears again in fire, but this fire does not drive a man away to his death. It calls him by name and sends him to rescue others.

The passage answers a question left hanging since Genesis 15: how will God keep His word to Abraham about the land and the nations? The patriarchs knew God as God Almighty, but they had not seen the fullness of what His name would mean, Exodus 6:3. Here God reveals the name that will carry Israel's faith, and He attaches it to action. From now on, 'the LORD' will mean the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, Exodus 20:2.

It also sets up everything to come. The sign of 3:12 points to Sinai: Israel will worship on this very mountain. There the fire of the bush becomes the fire on the mountain, Exodus 19:18, and then the glory filling the tabernacle, Exodus 40:34. The God who dwelt in a bush will dwell in a tent in the middle of His people. The whole movement of Exodus is from God meeting one man in the wilderness to God living among a nation.

The story reaches its centre in Jesus, who takes the name of the bush on His own lips, John 8:58, and in whom God came down not in a flame but in flesh, John 1:14. He is the sent one who never refused. Through His death and resurrection He brings His people out of a slavery deeper than Egypt's, and through Him believers call on the name of the Lord and are saved, Romans 10:13.

The story ends in the new creation. Moses had to hide his face, but in the city to come God's servants 'will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4. The name first spoken from a bush in the wilderness will be written on the people God has redeemed, and the God who said 'I will be with you' will dwell with them forever, Revelation 21:3.

sermon.title: 'I Am Who I Am'
sermon.why: Piper works directly through Exodus 3:13-15, unpacking the divine name I AM WHO I AM and the name YHWH built from it, showing why God's absolute, self-existent being is the foundation for everything else Scripture reveals about Him. A clear, orthodox exposition of this exact passage.

quiz.q: What was significant about the bush Moses saw at Horeb?

options.text: It was ablaze with fire yet was not consumed, marking God's holy presence.
options.note: Verse 2 records this detail, and it draws Moses to turn aside and see, leading to God's call from within it.

options.text: It was simply an ordinary desert fire.
options.note: The text emphasizes its extraordinary nature, a fire that does not consume.

options.text: Moses set the bush on fire himself.
options.note: The fire and the voice both originate from God, not from Moses.

options.text: It had burned to ashes when Moses arrived.
options.note: The remarkable detail is precisely that it was not consumed despite burning.

quiz.q: What name does God reveal to Moses when asked what he should tell the Israelites?

options.text: The God of the Egyptians.
options.note: This contradicts the passage; God identifies Himself as the God of Israel's fathers, not of Egypt.

options.text: No name is given in this passage.
options.note: The name I AM WHO I AM and the LORD are both explicitly given.

options.text: God Almighty, the name He used with Abraham.
options.note: That name, El Shaddai, is referenced later in Exodus 6:3, but here God reveals the new, deeper name I AM.

options.text: I AM WHO I AM, from which comes the name the LORD, YHWH.
options.note: Verses 14 to 15 record this revelation directly, God's self-existent, covenant name forever.

quiz.q: How many times did Moses object to God's commission, and how did God respond?

options.text: Moses objected once and God refused to answer.
options.note: God patiently answers every one of Moses' repeated objections with reassurance and signs.

options.text: Moses raised repeated objections about his worthiness, credibility, and speaking ability, and God patiently answered each with reassurance and signs.
options.note: Moses objects in 3:11, 3:13, 4:1, and 4:10, and God answers each, finally appointing Aaron in 4:14-16.

options.text: God rejected Moses for objecting and chose someone else entirely.
options.note: God grows angry at 4:14 but still sends Moses, pairing him with Aaron rather than replacing him.

options.text: Moses accepted the call immediately without hesitation.
options.note: The text records the opposite; Moses raises multiple objections before finally going.

quiz.q: What three signs did God give Moses to authenticate his calling?

options.text: Splitting the sea, providing manna, and giving the law.
options.note: Those events come much later in the exodus story, not as signs given here at the burning bush.

options.text: Healing the sick and raising the dead.
options.note: These are not the signs recorded in this passage.

options.text: No signs were given to Moses.
options.note: Three specific signs are explicitly given in verses 4:2-9.

options.text: The staff turning into a snake, his hand becoming leprous and being restored, and water from the Nile turning to blood.
options.note: Verses 4:2-9 describe these three signs given for Israel to believe Moses was sent by God.

quiz.q: Why is God's self-revelation as I AM significant for the mission Moses is given?

options.text: It reveals that God's plans depend on Moses' eloquence.
options.note: God explicitly answers Moses' concern about eloquence by asserting His own sovereignty over human speech, verse 4:11.

options.text: It is simply a poetic title with no bearing on the mission.
options.note: The name is directly tied to the promise of deliverance and God's covenant faithfulness, not merely decorative language.

options.text: It means God is distant and uninvolved in the mission.
options.note: The whole passage shows God intimately involved, coming down to rescue and commissioning Moses personally.

options.text: It grounds Israel's deliverance in God's own unchanging, self-existent, covenant-keeping character rather than in Moses' ability.
options.note: The name assures Moses and Israel that the mission rests on who God is, not on human qualification.

questions: Moses stood on holy ground because of God's presence, not because of anything special about the dirt. Where in your ordinary week might God be present in a way you have not paused to notice?

God said, I AM WHO I AM, grounding Moses' mission in His own unchanging character. When you feel unqualified for what God is asking of you, how does resting in who God is, rather than who you are, change your confidence?
Moses raised objection after objection, and God patiently kept answering rather than giving up on him. Where do you need to bring your honest doubts to God rather than hiding them?
God said He had seen, heard, and known Israel's affliction long before He acted. What suffering in your life or in someone else's do you need to trust that God has truly seen and heard?
God provided Aaron to help Moses speak, showing that His call often comes with provision we did not expect. Where might God be providing help for a task you feel unequipped to do alone?

translationNotes.note: Ehyeh asher ehyeh can be rendered I AM WHO I AM or I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE, since the Hebrew imperfect can carry ongoing being or unfolding future action; both senses assure Israel of God's reliable, active presence.

The phrase rendered unless a mighty hand compels him is literally except by a mighty hand, which some read as God's hand of judgment forcing Pharaoh's release rather than Pharaoh acting under any hand but his own.

The staff becomes a nachash, an ordinary snake, in contrast to Aaron's staff, which becomes a tannin, a larger serpent or monster, before Pharaoh in Exodus 7:10, a distinct and more dramatic sign for that royal audience.
